title: More, Less, Fewer
overview: This unit is about amounts, and about words for things you cannot touch. You will say less water and fewer bottles, and compare with harder, sooner and the earliest. You will learn the small word that comes before a noun: by bus, in cash, at once. It is the last unit of this stage, so the quiz looks back at Units 8 to 13.
learningPath: Meet 30 words for amounts, for feelings and for how a service works.
Read a short text, an information page and a real notice.
Learn both, all, less, fewer, not as many, not as much.
Compare the way you do things: harder, sooner, the earliest.
Learn the fixed phrases: by bus, in cash, on foot, at once.
Name what you cannot touch, and join two nouns into one.
Speak, write by hand, and check every answer against the key.
Take the checkpoint quiz, then record your stage assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 14. This unit is about amounts.
It is also about words for things you cannot touch.
This is the last unit of the stage, so you will meet Units 8 to 13 again at the end.
Start with the words for amounts.
Less and fewer both mean a smaller quantity. They do not go with the same nouns.
Fewer goes with things you can count. Fewer bottles. Fewer people. Fewer days.
Less goes with things you cannot count. Less water. Less sugar. Less noise.
The majority is more than half of a group. The minority is less than half.
The total is everything added together.
The average is the middle amount. You add the numbers, then you share them out equally.
Extra means more than the usual amount.
The maximum is the largest amount that is allowed.
Now the first pattern.
Both means the two of them. Both bags are heavy.
All means every one, or the whole of it.
All the bags are heavy. All the water is cold.
Not as many and not as much are a quiet way to compare downwards.
I bought fewer eggs this week. I bought not as many eggs as last week.
Not as many goes with countable nouns. Not as much goes with uncountable ones.
The second pattern is about how you do a thing.
You already say more slowly and the most carefully.
Some short words do not take more. They add -er and -est instead.
Hard, harder, the hardest. Soon, sooner, the soonest.
Early, earlier, the earliest. Fast, faster, the fastest.
Late, later, the latest. Long, longer, the longest.
I worked harder this month. The bus came sooner than I expected.
Her train leaves the earliest, at five.
These words say how, not what. They come after the verb.
The third pattern is a small word before a noun.
By bus. By car. By post. By hand. On foot. On time.
In cash. In person. At once. At first. At work. For free.
These are fixed. You do not work them out. You learn each one whole.
I come to work by bus, but on Friday I come on foot.
Can I pay in cash? Yes, or by card.
Please sign the form in person, not by post.
Come at once means come now.
The fourth pattern names things you cannot touch.
Kind is a describing word. Kindness is the thing itself.
Safe becomes safety. Free becomes freedom. Honest becomes honesty.
Patient becomes patience. Loyal becomes loyalty.
Succeed becomes success. Fail becomes failure.
You cannot hold kindness in your hand. You can see it in what people do.
These words are usually uncountable, so they take less and not fewer.
There is less patience in that queue than in this one.
The same card joins two nouns into one word.
Sun and shine make sunshine. Time and table make timetable.
Tooth and brush make toothbrush. News and paper make newspaper.
Work and place make workplace. Post and code make postcode.
Hand and bag make handbag. Key and board make keyboard.
Look for the two words inside. They usually tell you the meaning.
A workplace is a place where you work. A toothbrush is a brush for your teeth.
This is the last unit of the stage, so the quiz looks back.
Six of the twelve questions come from Units 8 to 13.
Be ready for for and since. Be ready for bored and boring.
Be ready for mustn't and need, and for polite would and could.
Be ready for if you heat ice, it melts.
Be ready for I was cooking when the power went off.
Work through the four cards in order.
Do the practice, then check every answer against the key.
Record yourself, listen back, and compare with the model.
Write one task by hand, on paper, and read it back a day later.
You can do all of this alone. Start now.

words.meaning: A smaller amount of something you cannot count.
words.example: Use less water when you wash the plates.
practice: There is less noise here after seven.
I put less sugar in my tea now.
We had less rain this month than last month.
Try to spend less time on the phone.
words.tutor: Give me six nouns, one at a time, and ask me to say less or fewer before each one.

words.meaning: A smaller number of things you can count.
words.example: Fewer people came on Saturday.
practice: I bought fewer eggs this week.
There are fewer buses after nine at night.
We need fewer chairs, not more.
Fewer staff work on a Sunday.
words.tutor: Ask me to say four sentences with fewer, and tell me if any noun in them cannot be counted.

words.meaning: More than half of a group of people or things.
words.example: The majority of the class arrived on time.
practice: The majority of our food comes from one shop.
A majority voted for the later time.
The majority of the seats were empty.
In the majority of cases, the form is enough.
words.tutor: Give me a group of ten people and tell me how many agreed, then ask me whether that is a majority.

words.meaning: Less than half of a group; the smaller part of it.
words.example: Only a minority pay by card here.
practice: A small minority of the staff work at night.
The minority asked for an earlier start.
A minority of the food comes from the garden.
In a minority of cases we send it by post.
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between a majority and a minority, and give me two numbers to test my answer.

words.meaning: The middle amount: add the numbers, then share them out equally.
words.example: The average is nine minutes.
practice: Work out the average of these four numbers.
The average wait on Monday is short.
That price is above the average.
Our average for the week was twenty.
words.tutor: Give me four numbers and ask me to say the average in a full sentence.

words.meaning: The whole amount, when everything is added together.
words.example: The total is forty.
practice: Write the total at the bottom of the form.
What is the total for both bags?
The total came to less than I expected.
Check the total before you pay.
words.tutor: Read me three prices, then ask me for the total and check my number.

words.meaning: More than the usual amount, or more than you need.
words.example: I worked an extra hour on Tuesday.
practice: Bring an extra bag if you can.
There is no extra cost for delivery.
She asked for an extra day.
We keep an extra key at the desk.
words.tutor: Ask me four questions that begin with Is there an extra, and check I answer in full sentences.

words.meaning: The largest amount that is allowed or possible.
words.example: The maximum is four bags.
practice: Two hours is the maximum for parking here.
What is the maximum number of people?
The notice gives a maximum of one meal.
Stay under the maximum and you will be fine.
words.tutor: Give me a notice with a limit on it, and ask me to say the maximum in my own words.

words.meaning: What a person shows when they help somebody for nothing.
words.example: A stranger carried my bag up the steps, and I still remember that kindness.
practice: Her kindness made a hard day easier.
Small acts of kindness cost nothing.
There was a lot of kindness in that room.
I wrote a note to thank them for their kindness.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe one act of kindness in three sentences, then check I used the noun and not the word kind.

words.meaning: What you have when you wait a long time and stay calm.
words.example: Thank you for your patience; the queue is long today.
practice: This job needs patience.
I lost my patience at the counter.
She has more patience than I have.
There is less patience in that queue than in this one.
words.tutor: Ask me when I need patience and when I lose it, and tell me if I used the noun both times.

words.meaning: Telling people what is true, even when it costs you something.
words.example: Her honesty at the desk saved us an hour.
practice: Honesty is easier in the end.
He told me with complete honesty.
The form asks for honesty, not for a good story.
There was honesty in her answer, and I trusted it.
words.tutor: Ask me to say what honesty is without using the word honest, then tell me if I managed it.

words.meaning: Being able to choose what you do, with nobody stopping you.
words.example: Working at night gives me the freedom to study by day.
practice: She has the freedom to choose her own hours.
Freedom to leave early matters to me.
The new timetable gives us more freedom.
I would swap money for freedom.
words.tutor: Ask me for two kinds of freedom I would like in a week, and check both answers use the noun.

words.meaning: Being away from danger, so that nothing can hurt you.
words.example: The helmet is there for your safety.
practice: Safety comes before speed.
Read the safety notice on the door.
We checked the tools for safety.
Her safety mattered more than the delivery.
words.tutor: Ask me three safety rules for a place I know, and tell me if any rule is not about danger.

words.meaning: Staying beside the same person or group, in good times and in bad ones.
words.example: Her loyalty to her team was clear.
practice: Loyalty takes years to build.
He showed loyalty when nobody else did.
The shop gives a small gift for loyalty.
There is more loyalty here than in my last workplace.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe loyalty in three sentences without using the word loyal.

words.meaning: Getting the result you were working for.
words.example: The evening was a success.
practice: Success took her three attempts.
The delivery service is a success.
For me, success is a quiet week.
We had some success with the new method.
words.tutor: Ask me what success means to me this month, then ask me for one step towards it.

words.meaning: Not getting the result you were working for.
words.example: The first attempt was a failure, and the second one worked.
practice: A failure teaches you something.
Nobody calls one bad day a failure.
The failure was in the method, not in the people.
After two failures, she changed her plan.
words.tutor: Ask me to say one failure and what I learned from it, in two sentences.

words.meaning: The light and the heat that come from the sun.
words.example: There was sunshine all afternoon.
practice: We had less sunshine this week.
Sit in the sunshine for ten minutes.
The sunshine came through the window.
Sunshine is not the same as warm air.
words.tutor: Ask me which two words make sunshine, and then ask me for one more word that starts with sun.

words.meaning: A list of times: when a bus goes, or when a class starts.
words.example: The timetable is on the door.
practice: Check the timetable before you leave.
The timetable changes on Monday.
I copied the timetable onto paper.
There are fewer buses on the Sunday timetable.
words.tutor: Ask me to read a timetable aloud, then ask me one question about the earliest time on it.

words.meaning: A small brush for cleaning your teeth.
words.example: Pack a toothbrush and some soap.
practice: My toothbrush is in the blue bag.
Buy a new toothbrush every three months.
A toothbrush costs less than a comb here.
She put the toothbrush beside the sink.
words.tutor: Ask me which two words make toothbrush, and ask me for two more words that end with brush.

words.meaning: Large sheets of paper with the day's news printed on them.
words.example: He reads a newspaper on the bus.
practice: The newspaper comes by delivery at six.
Fewer people buy a newspaper now.
I saw the notice in the newspaper.
Wrap the glass in old newspaper.
words.tutor: Ask me what a newspaper is made of and what is in it, using the two words inside the word.

words.meaning: The building or the room where a person does their job.
words.example: Safety rules are on the wall in every workplace.
practice: My workplace is ten minutes away on foot.
There is more kindness in this workplace.
A good workplace has clear rules.
She changed workplace in March.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a workplace, or the place where I study, in four sentences.

words.meaning: The short set of letters or numbers at the end of an address.
words.example: Write the postcode under the street name.
practice: The form will not send without a postcode.
What is the postcode there?
I always forget the last part of the postcode.
Two streets can share one postcode.
words.tutor: Ask me for a made-up address with a postcode, and check that I put the postcode last.

words.meaning: A small bag you carry, with your keys, your money and your phone in it.
words.example: Her handbag was on the chair.
practice: Keep your handbag closed on the bus.
I found the card in my handbag.
That handbag is too small for a newspaper.
He handed her the handbag at the desk.
words.tutor: Ask me to name five things in a handbag, then ask me which two words make the word.

words.meaning: The flat set of keys you press to write on a computer.
words.example: The keyboard needs cleaning.
practice: I type faster on a big keyboard.
Water fell on the keyboard and it stopped.
The keyboard on my phone is very small.
Press the same key on any keyboard.
words.tutor: Ask me which two words make keyboard, and ask me how the word board helps me guess the meaning.

words.meaning: A way of doing something, with steps in a fixed order.
words.example: Her method is quicker than mine.
practice: Follow the same method every time.
We changed the method last month.
Which method of payment do you take?
The method has four steps.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a method in four steps, then tell me if any step is out of order.

words.meaning: The buses, trains, cars and planes that move people and things.
words.example: Public transport stops at midnight here.
practice: Transport costs less with a weekly ticket.
There is no transport to the door.
We use transport for the heavy bags only.
What transport do you take to work?
words.tutor: Ask me three questions about the transport I use, and check I answer with by plus a noun.

words.meaning: Money you give for something, or the act of giving it.
words.example: We take payment at the counter.
practice: Payment by card is quicker.
The first payment is due on Friday.
They cannot take payment by post.
Keep the receipt as proof of payment.
words.tutor: Play a person at a counter. Ask me how I want to make the payment and check my answer uses in or by.

words.meaning: Bringing something to the door of the person who wants it.
words.example: The delivery arrives before ten.
practice: There is no extra cost for delivery.
The shop has one delivery a week.
I missed the delivery on Tuesday.
Ask for delivery to your workplace.
words.tutor: Ask me four questions about a delivery, and tell me if any answer is not a full sentence.

words.meaning: Work that one person or one company does for other people.
words.example: The bus service is good in the morning.
practice: The service was slow, but everyone was kind.
There is a free service for older people.
Which service do you use for your post?
A new service starts in April.
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a service I use, in four sentences, and check I used the word service twice.

words.meaning: A way in, or permission to use something.
words.example: There is step-free access at the side door.
practice: Access to the garden is through the kitchen.
I have no access to that file.
The notice shows where the access is.
Ask at the desk about access after six.
words.tutor: Ask me where the access is in a building I know, and whether anybody is stopped from using it.

grammar.title: Fewer bottles, less water: both, all, not as many
grammar.explanation: You already know some, any, many and much. Now you need the smaller side. Fewer goes with nouns you can count. Less goes with nouns you cannot count. Both means the two of them, and all means every one, or the whole of it.
grammar.rule:
Count them? Use fewer.
Fewer bottles. Fewer people. Fewer buses. Fewer days.
Cannot count them? Use less.
Less water. Less sugar. Less noise. Less patience.
Both is for exactly two:
Both bags are heavy. I read both notices.
All is for every one, or for the whole of it:
All the bags are heavy. All the water is cold.
Compare downwards with as:
not as many + countable: I bought not as many eggs as last week.
not as much + uncountable: I use not as much water as you.
Two short tests.
Can you put a number in front of it? Then it is countable.
Can you put a in front of it? Then it is countable.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: We had ______ rain this month.
Ask: can I count rain?
Try a number: two rains. No.
Try a: a rain. No.
So rain is uncountable.
Uncountable takes less, never fewer.
Answer: We had less rain this month.
Now change the noun to days.
Two days works, so days is countable.
Answer: We had fewer days this month.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to say less people, because you hear it often. People can be counted, so English wants fewer here. Say: Fewer people came on Saturday.
grammar.tip: If you can count it, use fewer. If you can only weigh it or pour it, use less.
grammar.practice:
Write less or fewer.
1. There are ______ buses after nine.
2. Put ______ sugar in my tea, please.
3. ______ staff work on a Sunday.
4. We had ______ rain this month.
5. I have ______ patience than my sister.
6. She bought ______ eggs this week.
7. There is ______ noise here after seven.
8. ______ people pay in cash now.
grammar.answers:
1. fewer 2. less 3. fewer 4. less 5. less 6. fewer 7. less 8. fewer
The likeliest wrong answer is 8: writing less people. People is a plural of person, so you can count it. Fewer is right.
Item 5 catches people the other way. Patience is a thing you cannot count, so it takes less.

grammar.title: Harder, sooner, earliest: comparing how you do it
grammar.explanation: You already say more slowly and the most carefully. Some short words do not take more. They add -er and -est, exactly as short describing words do. These words say how something is done, so they come after the verb.
grammar.rule:
hard, harder, the hardest
soon, sooner, the soonest
early, earlier, the earliest
late, later, the latest
fast, faster, the fastest
long, longer, the longest
near, nearer, the nearest
I worked harder this month.
The bus came sooner than I expected.
Her train leaves the earliest, at five.
He finished the fastest of the three.
Two that change shape:
well, better, the best. I sleep better at the weekend.
badly, worse, the worst. The phone works worse in the rain.
Use than after the comparing form.
Use the before the -est form.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: The 41 bus comes ______ than the 12. (soon)
Ask: is soon a short word?
Yes, one syllable, so it takes -er.
So the form is sooner, not more soon.
There are two buses here, so it is a comparison, not a top one.
The word than is already in the sentence, and that is the sign.
Answer: The 41 bus comes sooner than the 12.
Now change it to three buses and the top one.
Answer: The 41 bus comes the soonest.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write more sooner or more harder. Choose one way only: either -er, or more, never both. Write: The bus came sooner than I expected.
grammar.tip: Short word, add -er and -est. Longer word, use more and the most. Than for two, the for the top one.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form of the word in brackets.
1. I worked ______ (hard) this month than last month.
2. She finished ______ (fast) of all six.
3. The post arrives ______ (early) on a Tuesday than on a Friday.
4. My train leaves ______ (early) of the three.
5. He sleeps ______ (well) at the weekend.
6. The bus came ______ (soon) than the notice said.
7. I waited ______ (long) than you did.
8. The signal works ______ (badly) in the rain than in the sun.
grammar.answers:
1. harder 2. the fastest 3. earlier 4. the earliest 5. better 6. sooner 7. longer 8. worse
The likeliest wrong answer is 5: writing more well. Well does not take more; it changes shape to better.
Items 2 and 4 both need the, because each one picks the top of a group. Item 4 also keeps the -est ending: the earliest.

grammar.title: By bus, in cash, at once: fixed phrases for how
grammar.explanation: English puts a small word in front of some nouns to say how a thing is done. These phrases are fixed. You cannot work them out from the meaning, and there is no the inside them. Learn each one whole, as if it were one word.
grammar.rule:
by, for the way it travels or the means:
by bus, by car, by train, by post, by card, by hand
on, for two that do not take by:
on foot, on time, on the phone
in, for the form a thing takes:
in cash, in person, in English, in writing, in a hurry
at, for a point:
at once, at first, at work, at home, at night
for, for what it costs:
for free, for nothing
I come to work by bus, but on Friday I come on foot.
Can I pay in cash? Yes, or by card.
Please sign the form in person, not by post.
Come at once. That means come now.
No the: say by bus, never by the bus.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: I always pay ______ cash at that shop.
Ask: is this about the means, the form or a point in time?
Cash is the form the money takes, not a vehicle.
The word for a form is in.
Check for the: in cash has no the.
Answer: I always pay in cash at that shop.
Now change cash to card.
A card is the means, so the phrase is by card.
Answer: I always pay by card at that shop.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to add the: I came by the bus. These phrases never take the. Write: I came by bus.
grammar.tip: By for the means, in for the form, on for foot and time, at for a point. No the inside any of them.
grammar.practice:
Write by, in, on, at or for.
1. I go to my workplace ______ foot.
2. Can I pay ______ cash?
3. Send the form ______ post, or bring it ______ person.
4. The delivery came ______ time.
5. Come ______ once; the queue is short now.
6. She wrote the whole list ______ hand.
7. The second bag is ______ free.
8. ______ first I went ______ bus, and later I walked.
grammar.answers:
1. on 2. in 3. by, in 4. on 5. at 6. by 7. for 8. At, by
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing by foot. Feet are not a vehicle, and English fixed this one as on foot.
Item 6 catches people too. By hand means a person did it, not a machine. In hand means something else, so the two are not the same.

grammar.title: Kindness, sunshine: a feeling named, two nouns joined
grammar.explanation: Some nouns name things you cannot touch: kindness, safety, freedom. Many are built from a describing word with an ending. Other nouns are two words pushed into one: sunshine, timetable. The two words inside usually give you the meaning.
grammar.rule:
Describing word, then the noun built from it:
kind, kindness. safe, safety. honest, honesty.
patient, patience. loyal, loyalty. free, freedom.
Verb, then the noun:
succeed, success. fail, failure. pay, payment. deliver, delivery.
You cannot hold kindness, and you cannot count it.
So these nouns take less, not fewer:
There is less patience in that queue than in this one.
Two nouns joined into one word:
sun and shine make sunshine.
time and table make timetable.
tooth and brush make toothbrush.
news and paper make newspaper.
work and place make workplace.
hand and bag make handbag.
key and board make keyboard.
post and code make postcode.
The second word says what it is. The first word says which kind.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: He waited an hour and stayed calm. What did he show? (patient)
Ask: do I need the describing word or the noun?
The sentence asks what he showed, so I need a thing. That is a noun.
Patient ends in -t. The noun changes the ending to -ence.
Answer: He showed patience.
Now do a joined noun.
Item: a brush for your teeth.
The second word says what it is: a brush.
The first word says which kind: tooth.
Answer: a toothbrush.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to use the describing word where the noun belongs: She showed kind. English needs the noun there. Write: She showed kindness.
grammar.tip: If you can point at it, it is a thing you can count. If you can only see it in what people do, it takes less.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Write the noun built from the word in brackets.
1. She showed great ______ (kind) at the desk.
2. Read the ______ (safe) notice on the door.
3. The evening was a ______ (succeed).
4. Thank you for your ______ (patient).
Part B. Write the two words inside each noun.
5. sunshine
6. workplace
7. keyboard
8. newspaper
grammar.answers:
Part A: 1. kindness 2. safety 3. success 4. patience
Part B: 5. sun and shine 6. work and place 7. key and board 8. news and paper
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing succeed. The sentence needs a thing after a, so it must be the noun success.
Item 2 loses its last letter: safe becomes safety, not safeity.

readings.title: Two shops on the same street
readings.setting: A kitchen, after work, two neighbours talking
readings.passage:
Eva puts her handbag on the table. Ivan is reading a newspaper.
'You are back sooner than usual,' he says.
'I went to the new shop,' says Eva. 'The one at the far end.'
'Is it better?'
'It is different. There are fewer people in it, so the queue is shorter.'
Ivan folds the paper. 'And the prices?'
'About the same. I paid less for the rice and more for the oil.'
'So the total is the same.'
'Almost,' says Eva. 'But I did not have to wait. The old shop is faster at the counter, and slower at the door.'
Ivan laughs. 'Both shops are on the same street.'
'Both shops are open until seven,' says Eva, 'but the new one opens the earliest. Six in the morning.'
'Do they take cash?'
'In cash or by card. And they have a delivery service on Thursday.'
'That is useful. Our stairs are hard with two bags.'
Eva sits down. 'The woman at the counter carried my bag to the door. I did not ask her.'
'That was kindness,' says Ivan.
'It was. I will go back for that alone.'

readings.title: How a delivery service works
readings.passage:
A delivery service takes a thing from a shop or a store and brings it to your door. Every service works the same way, in four steps.
Step one is the order. You choose what you want and give an address. The postcode matters most. A wrong postcode sends the driver to the wrong street.
Step two is the payment. Most services take payment by card when you order. A minority still take cash at the door. Ask first, because a driver who carries no change cannot help you.
Step three is the transport. Small things go by van. Heavy things go by lorry. In a busy street the last part is often on foot.
Step four is the delivery itself. The driver has a maximum number of stops in a day. The average is about sixty, and each stop takes three minutes.
That number explains the rest. A driver who waits four minutes at every door makes fewer stops, so the company asks you to answer quickly.
Access is the other half of the problem. A door with three steps and no bell takes longer than a door with a ramp. If you have a side door, say so when you order.
Safety comes first for a heavy box. A driver may refuse to carry it up the stairs, and that is a rule, not a lack of kindness.
If nobody is at home, most services try again the next day. After two failures the box goes back to the store, and you collect it in person.

readings.title: Community kitchen: notice for users
readings.setting: A board beside the door of a community kitchen
readings.passage:
COMMUNITY KITCHEN: NOTICE FOR USERS
14 Mill Road. Postcode: 3120.

TIMETABLE
Monday to Friday: 8 in the morning until 7 at night.
Saturday: 9 until 2. Closed on Sunday.
We do not take bookings. Come at once if you need a hot meal.

HOW MANY
Maximum four hot meals per person per day.
Maximum two bags of dry food per household each week.
If you take fewer bags, you may come back sooner.
On Saturday we serve less hot food, because fewer staff work that day.

PAYMENT
Hot meals are free. Dry food costs 2 for one bag.
You may pay in cash at the counter, or by card.
We cannot take payment by post.

ACCESS
The front door has three steps. The side door on Mill Road has none.
Ring the bell at the side door and somebody will open it.

TRANSPORT
The 41 bus stops outside. On foot from the station it takes about nine minutes.
Parking is for delivery vans only.

HELP US
The majority of our food comes from shops on this street.
A small minority comes from our own garden.
If you can give an extra hour on a Tuesday, please ask at the counter.
Thank you for your patience when the queue is long.

comprehension.q: Why is the queue shorter at the new shop?
comprehension.a: Because there are fewer people in it.
comprehension.why: Eva says: There are fewer people in it, so the queue is shorter. People can be counted, so the word is fewer.

comprehension.q: Which shop opens the earliest, and at what time?
comprehension.a: The new shop, at six in the morning.
comprehension.why: Eva says both shops close at seven, but the new one opens the earliest, at six in the morning.

comprehension.q: Eva says she paid less for the rice and more for the oil. Why does Ivan say the total is the same?
comprehension.a: Because what she saved on the rice she spent on the oil, so the whole amount did not change.
comprehension.why: The total is everything added together. One price went down and the other went up by about the same amount.

comprehension.q: The woman carried Eva's bag without being asked. Which noun does Ivan use for that?
comprehension.why: Ivan says: That was kindness. It is the noun built from kind, and it names something you cannot touch.

comprehension.q: What are the four steps of a delivery service, in order?
comprehension.a: The order, the payment, the transport, and the delivery itself.
comprehension.why: The text numbers them: step one is the order, step two the payment, step three the transport, step four the delivery.

comprehension.q: Why does the company ask you to answer the door quickly?
comprehension.a: Because a driver who waits at every door makes fewer stops in the day.
comprehension.why: The text gives an average of sixty stops at three minutes each. Four minutes at every door would cut that number.

comprehension.q: The text says access is the other half of the problem. What does access mean here?
comprehension.a: The way in to the building, and how easy it is to use.
comprehension.why: The sentences beside it talk about steps, a bell and a ramp, so access is about getting in.

comprehension.q: You have two people in your household and you want dry food. What is the maximum you may take in one week?
comprehension.a: Two bags. The limit is per household, not per person.
comprehension.why: The notice says maximum two bags of dry food per household each week, so two people share the same two bags.

comprehension.q: You cannot use steps. Which door do you use, and what do you do there?
comprehension.a: The side door on Mill Road, and you ring the bell.
comprehension.why: The notice says the front door has three steps and the side door has none, and that you ring the bell there.

comprehension.q: It is Saturday at half past two and you want a hot meal. What can you do?
comprehension.a: Nothing today: on Saturday the kitchen closes at 2. Go back on Monday from 8 in the morning.
comprehension.why: The timetable gives Saturday as 9 until 2, and Sunday as closed, so Monday morning is the next opening.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Less, fewer, both, all
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
There are fewer buses after nine.
I use less water than I did last year.
Fewer people came on Saturday.
There is less noise in this street.
Both bags are heavy.
All the water is cold.
I bought not as many eggs as last week.
I use not as much sugar as you.
Now make eight of your own about your week.
Use fewer four times and less four times.
Play back your recording.
Check one thing: is every noun after fewer a plural you can count?
Say any line again if you used less with a plural.
speaking.tutor: Read me eight sentences with less and fewer, and tell me which ones used the wrong word and why.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Harder, sooner, the earliest
speaking.instructions:
Read each question, then say your answer out loud.
Which bus comes sooner, the 41 or the 12?
Who finished the fastest last week?
Did you work harder this month or last month?
Which shop opens the earliest near you?
Do you sleep better at the weekend?
You may invent every answer.
Use than in three answers and the in two.
Record the five answers. Play them back.
Check: did you say more harder or more sooner anywhere?
If you did, say that answer again with the -er form alone.
speaking.tutor: Ask me five questions that need harder, sooner, earlier, faster or better, and tell me if I ever used more with them.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Listen to the short talk
speaking.instructions:
Play Reading 2, How a delivery service works. Listen without looking at the page.
Listen for five main points. Write each one down in a few words.
1. How many steps the service has.
2. What matters most in the address.
3. How most people pay.
4. The average number of stops in a day.
5. What happens after two failures.
Now look at Reading 2 and check your five answers.
The answers are: four steps; the postcode; by card; about sixty; the box goes back to the store.
Five out of five? Move on.
Fewer? Play it once more and listen only for the ones you missed.
Then say the five points out loud, record them, and play them back.
speaking.tutor: Read the delivery text to me slowly, then ask me five questions about its main points.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — At the counter
speaking.instructions:
You are at a counter. Say both halves out loud, twice each.
Can I pay in cash? Yes, in cash or by card.
How do I send the form? By post, or bring it in person.
How do you come to work? On foot, or by bus when it rains.
When do you need it? At once, please.
Is there a second bag? Yes, and it is for free.
Record all ten lines. Play them back.
Check: did you say the inside any phrase?
By the bus and on the foot are both wrong. Say that line again.
If somebody is with you, let them read the first half.
You do not need them. The lines above are the other half.
speaking.tutor: Play the person at a counter. Ask me four questions about payment and transport, and check my small words.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Two months, compared
speaking.instructions:
Talk for one minute about two months: this one and an earlier one. You may invent both.
Use at least four of these six:
harder, sooner, earlier, the earliest, better, longer.
Use less or fewer at least twice.
Here is a model. Read it first, then say your own.
I worked harder this month than in March.
I started earlier, at seven, and I finished later.
There were fewer quiet days and less sunshine.
But I slept better, because I came home sooner.
The earliest I left the house was half past five.
Record yourself. Play it back and count the forms you used.
Four of the six, and two of less or fewer, is a pass.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my one minute about two months and tell me which comparing forms I used and which I missed.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Ask about a service
speaking.instructions:
Ask six questions about a service. Then answer each one yourself, in a full sentence.
Model questions:
What is the maximum I can take?
Can I pay in cash?
Is there access without steps?
What time is the earliest delivery?
Do I have to come in person?
Is the second one for free?
Record the six questions and the six answers. Play it back.
Check two things.
Did every question with how or what start with a question word?
Did every answer keep the small word: in cash, on foot, at once, for free?
Say again any answer that lost its small word.
speaking.tutor: Ask me six questions about a service you invent, one at a time, and tell me if any answer is not a full sentence.

writing.title: Writing 1 — This week and last week
writing.prompt: Write four sentences comparing this week with last week. You may invent both weeks. Use fewer twice and less twice. End one sentence with a comparison using as.
writing.model:
This week I took fewer buses, because I walked on Tuesday.
I drank less coffee and slept more.
There were fewer people at the shop on Thursday.
I spent not as much money as last week.
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Fewer used twice, with a plural noun each time. Less used twice, with a noun you cannot count. Every sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
writing.support: Write only the four nouns first, one per line: buses, coffee, people, money. Then ask of each one: can I count it? Write fewer or less beside it, and only then write the sentence.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence with both or all, about two things that were the same in both weeks.

writing.title: Writing 2 — What this place gives me
writing.prompt: Write five sentences about a place you know: a workplace, a shop, a clinic, or where you study. You may invent it. Use three nouns for things you cannot touch, from kindness, patience, honesty, freedom, safety, loyalty, success, failure. Use two joined nouns, from timetable, workplace, newspaper, keyboard, handbag, postcode, toothbrush, sunshine.
writing.model:
My workplace is small, and there is a lot of kindness in it.
The timetable is on the door, and it changes every Monday.
Safety matters here, so we read the notice before we start.
My first month was a failure, and the second one went better.
I have the freedom to swap a shift, and that is why I stay.
writing.criteria: Five sentences. Three nouns for things you cannot touch. Two joined nouns. No describing word used where the noun belongs: kindness, not kind. Every sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
writing.support: Write the five nouns down the page first, one per line. Then finish each line into a sentence. Choosing the words before the sentences is the whole job.
writing.extension: Add one sentence with less plus a noun you cannot touch, for example: There is less noise here than at my last workplace.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A card, written by hand
writing.prompt:
Write this one on paper, with a pen.
Write six lines about how you get somewhere and how you pay for it.
It can be a real journey or an invented one.
Use four fixed phrases from this list:
by bus, by car, by post, by hand, on foot,
on time, in cash, in person, at once, for free.
Write at a normal speed, not slowly.
writing.model:
I go to the market by bus on Saturday.
If the bus is late, I walk the last part on foot.
I pay in cash, because the small shops prefer it.
The big shop takes payment by card, and the delivery is for free.
I order the heavy bags in person, not by post.
The delivery arrives on time, more often than not.
writing.criteria: Six lines, written by hand. Four fixed phrases, and no the inside any of them. Every line has a capital letter and a full stop. You can read every word of it back a day later.
writing.support: Write the four phrases on a separate line first, in your own handwriting. Look at them. If any letter is hard to read there, slow that letter down before you write the six lines.
writing.extension: Put the card away and read it again tomorrow. Circle any word you could not read at once, and write that word three more times.

writing.title: Writing 4 — The stage, in six sentences
writing.model:
I have worked at the same place since March.
The first week was tiring, and I was tired every night.
I think the job suits me, because the hours are fixed.
If I leave at six, I get the earlier bus.
I was cooking when the delivery came, so the food went cold.
This month I take fewer buses and spend less money.
writing.criteria: Six sentences, one for each of the six things listed. Each sentence has a capital letter and a full stop. The fifth sentence has two verbs: one with -ing and one in the past.
writing.support: Copy the six labels down the page first: since, tiring, I think, if, was -ing, fewer. Then write one sentence beside each label. Do not write them in order if one is easier.
writing.extension: Join two of your six sentences with so or when, and read the longer sentence out loud to check it still makes sense.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which amount word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: less, fewer, majority, minority, average, total, extra, maximum.
1. The ______ is four bags per household.
2. Add the three numbers and write the ______ at the bottom.
3. The ______ of our food comes from one shop; more than half.
4. Only a ______ pay in cash now; less than half.
5. I worked an ______ hour on Tuesday.
6. There are ______ buses after nine at night.
7. Put ______ sugar in it, please.
8. Add the four numbers, then share them out: that is the ______.
activities.answers:
1. maximum 2. total 3. majority 4. minority 5. extra 6. fewer 7. less 8. average
Seven or eight right: move on. Five or six: read the word cards for the ones you missed. Four or fewer: read all eight cards again, then do this once more.
Items 2 and 8 are the pair to study. The total is everything added. The average is the total shared out equally.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Less or fewer, much or many
activities.instructions:
Write less or fewer for items 1 to 4. Write not as much or not as many for items 5 to 8.
1. ______ people came on Sunday.
2. We had ______ rain in April.
3. There are ______ chairs in this room.
4. She has ______ patience than I have.
5. I bought ______ eggs as last week.
6. I use ______ water as my neighbour.
7. We had ______ visitors as in March.
8. There is ______ noise as there was before.
activities.answers:
1. fewer 2. less 3. fewer 4. less 5. not as many 6. not as much 7. not as many 8. not as much
Six or more right: move on. Fewer: go back to card 1 and use the two tests on each noun.
Item 4 is the one that catches people. Patience is a thing you cannot count, so it takes less, even though it feels like a quality somebody has more of.
activities.solo: Do items 1 to 4 with card 1 open beside you. Do items 5 to 8 with it closed.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Write the comparing form
activities.instructions:
Write the right form of the word in brackets.
1. The 41 bus comes ______ (soon) than the 12.
2. I worked ______ (hard) this month than last month.
3. Of all four shops, that one opens ______ (early).
4. He finished ______ (fast) of the six.
5. I sleep ______ (well) at the weekend than on a weekday.
6. The signal works ______ (badly) in the rain.
7. I waited ______ (long) than you did.
8. The post arrives ______ (late) on a Saturday.
activities.answers:
1. sooner 2. harder 3. the earliest 4. the fastest 5. better 6. worse 7. longer 8. later
Seven or eight right: move on. Fewer: read card 2 again, then do items 3, 4 and 5 once more.
Items 3 and 4 need the, because each one picks the top of a group. Items 1, 2, 5 and 7 have than, and than always means two.
activities.solo: Say each answer out loud before you write it. More harder is easy to hear as wrong, and hard to see as wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The small word
activities.instructions:
Write by, in, on, at or for in each gap.
1. I come to my workplace ______ foot.
2. Can I pay ______ cash, or do you need a card?
3. She wrote the whole list ______ hand.
4. Bring the form ______ person, please.
5. The delivery arrived ______ time.
6. Come ______ once; the counter closes in ten minutes.
7. The second bag is ______ free.
8. He sends everything ______ post, even now.
activities.answers:
1. on 2. in 3. by 4. in 5. on 6. at 7. for 8. by
Seven or eight right: move on. Fewer: read card 3 again and say each phrase out loud five times.
Item 1 is the commonest slip. On foot, never by foot.
Items 3 and 4 look alike and are not: by hand means a person did it, and in person means you came yourself.
activities.solo: Write the five small words across the top of your page first: by, in, on, at, for. Cross one out only when you are sure you have used it everywhere it belongs.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Build it and break it
activities.instructions:
Part A. Write the noun built from the word in brackets.
1. ______ (kind)
2. ______ (safe)
3. ______ (honest)
4. ______ (free)
5. ______ (patient)
6. ______ (loyal)
7. ______ (succeed)
8. ______ (fail)
Part B. Write the two words inside each noun.
9. sunshine
10. timetable
11. toothbrush
12. newspaper
13. workplace
14. postcode
15. handbag
16. keyboard
activities.answers:
Part A: 1. kindness 2. safety 3. honesty 4. freedom 5. patience 6. loyalty 7. success 8. failure
Part B: 9. sun and shine 10. time and table 11. tooth and brush 12. news and paper 13. work and place 14. post and code 15. hand and bag 16. key and board
Twelve or more of the sixteen: move on. Fewer: read card 4 again, then do Part A once more.
The endings in Part A are not all the same, and that is the difficulty. Four end in -ness, -ty or -y; free loses nothing and gains -dom; succeed and fail change more than an ending.
activities.solo: Do Part B first. It is easier, and it shows you that a long word is often two short ones you already know.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Read the notice
activities.instructions:
Use Reading 3 only. Write a short answer to each question.
1. What is the maximum number of hot meals for one person in a day?
2. How many bags of dry food may one household take in a week?
3. Why is there less hot food on a Saturday?
4. Which two ways can you pay?
5. Which door has no steps?
6. How long does it take on foot from the station?
7. Where does the majority of the food come from?
8. What time does the kitchen close on a Friday?
activities.answers:
1. Four. 2. Two. 3. Because fewer staff work on Saturday. 4. In cash at the counter, or by card. 5. The side door on Mill Road. 6. About nine minutes. 7. From shops on the same street. 8. At 7 at night.
Every answer is in the notice. If you could not find one, read the notice again with only that question in your head.
Item 2 is the trap: the limit is per household, not per person, so the number does not change with two people.
activities.solo: Answer from memory first. Then open the notice and mark the ones you got right. The gap between the two scores shows what to read more carefully.

quizzes.q: You want to say that this week you bought a smaller number of eggs. Which sentence is right?
options: I bought fewer eggs this week.
I bought less eggs this week.
I bought fewer egg this week.
I bought a less egg this week.
quizzes.a: I bought fewer eggs this week.
quizzes.why: Eggs can be counted, so the word is fewer. Less goes with things you cannot count, like water. Fewer needs the plural form eggs, not egg. The last one puts a in front of a smaller amount, which English does not do.

quizzes.q: Which sentence compares two amounts of water correctly?
options: I use not as many water as you.
I use not as much water as you.
I use not as fewer water as you.
I use not as less water as you.
quizzes.a: I use not as much water as you.
quizzes.why: Water cannot be counted, so the phrase is not as much. Not as many is for countable nouns. Fewer and less never follow as: the pair is as much or as many.

quizzes.q: Your bus arrived earlier than it usually does. Which sentence says it?
options: The bus came more soon than usual.
The bus came the soonest than usual.
The bus came sooner than usual.
The bus came more sooner than usual.
quizzes.a: The bus came sooner than usual.
quizzes.why: Soon is a short word, so it adds -er: sooner. More soon uses the long-word way instead. The soonest picks the top of a group and cannot take than. More sooner uses both ways at once.

quizzes.q: You walk to work. Which sentence is right?
options: I go to work by foot.
I go to work on bus.
I go to work with foot.
I go to work on foot.
quizzes.a: I go to work on foot.
quizzes.why: On foot is a fixed phrase and you learn it whole. By is for a vehicle, so by foot is wrong and on bus is wrong the other way round. With is for a tool you hold, not for walking.

quizzes.q: Somebody helped you for nothing. Which word names the thing they showed?
options: kindness
kind
kindly
kinder
quizzes.why: Kindness is the noun, and the sentence needs a thing. Kind is the describing word. Kindly says how something is done. Kinder compares two people.

quizzes.q: The word timetable is made of two words joined. Which two?
options: time and able
time and table
tim and etable
timet and able
quizzes.why: A timetable is a table of times, so the two words are time and table. Able is a different word and is not inside this one. The other two split the letters in places that make no words at all.

quizzes.q: You started this job in March, and you are still there. Which sentence is right?
options: I work here since March.
I have worked here for March.
I have worked here since March.
I have worked here since three months.
quizzes.a: I have worked here since March.
quizzes.why: Since names the point when it started, and something still true takes have worked. The first one uses the plain present, which does not reach back to March. For needs a length of time, not a month name, and since needs a point, not a length.

quizzes.q: Nothing happened in the film, and you fell asleep. How do you describe the film and yourself?
options: The film was bored, and I was boring.
The film was bored, and I was bored.
The film was boring, and I was boring.
The film was boring, and I was bored.
quizzes.a: The film was boring, and I was bored.
quizzes.why: The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling, so the film was boring. The -ed form describes the person who feels it, so you were bored. The other three swap one or both of them.

quizzes.q: There is a fire door, and people must never block it. Which sentence says that?
options: You mustn't block the fire door.
You don't need to block the fire door.
You needn't block the fire door.
You could block the fire door.
quizzes.a: You mustn't block the fire door.
quizzes.why: Mustn't says a thing is forbidden. Don't need to and needn't both say it is not necessary, which is the opposite of forbidden. Could says it is merely possible.

quizzes.q: Which sentence says what always happens?
options: If you will heat water enough, it boils.
If you heat water enough, it boils.
If you heated water enough, it boils.
If you heat water enough, it boiled.
quizzes.a: If you heat water enough, it boils.
quizzes.why: For something always true, both halves take the present simple. Will does not follow if in this pattern. The other two put one half in the past, which turns an always-true fact into one occasion.

quizzes.q: One action cut across another one. Which sentence is right?
options: I cooked when the power was going off.
I was cooking when the power was going off.
I was cooking when the power went off.
I cook when the power went off.
quizzes.a: I was cooking when the power went off.
quizzes.why: The long background action takes was plus -ing, and the short action that cuts across it takes the past simple. The first swaps them round. The second puts both in the long form, so nothing cuts across. The last one mixes present and past.

quizzes.q: The notice says the kitchen closes at 2 on Saturday. How do you report that fixed time?
options: The kitchen is closing at 2 on Saturday.
The kitchen will close at 2 on Saturday.
The kitchen is going to close at 2 on Saturday.
The kitchen closes at 2 on Saturday.
quizzes.a: The kitchen closes at 2 on Saturday.
quizzes.why: A time on a timetable or a notice takes the present simple. Is closing claims an arrangement somebody made with a person. Will close is a decision made as you speak. Going to needs a decision made earlier or something you can see coming.

teacherNotes.note: Less with a plural noun (less people, less bottles) is extremely common, and learners hear it from fluent speakers too, so telling them it is wrong rarely sticks. The two tests on grammar card 1 do more work than the rule: can you put a number in front of it, and can you put a in front of it. Run those two questions out loud over ten nouns and the choice stops being a guess.

The fixed phrases in card 3 cannot be reasoned out, and a learner who tries will keep producing by foot and on bus. Treat each phrase as one word. Five spoken repetitions of the whole phrase beat any explanation, and Practice 4 is built for that rather than for thinking.

The abstract nouns in card 4 do not all build the same way. Kind, honest and loyal take -ness, -y and -ty; safe loses its e before -ty; free takes -dom; succeed and fail change shape altogether. A learner who looks for one rule will find four. Practice 5 Part A is the list to learn as a list, and Part B is genuinely easy, so do Part B first when confidence is low.

Six of the twelve quiz items test Units 8 to 13, not this unit: for and since, -ing against -ed adjectives, mustn't against needn't, the zero conditional, past continuous cut across by past simple, and choosing a future form. A low quiz score here can therefore mean the earlier units, not this one. Read the six explanations item by item and send the learner back to the unit named there, rather than back to this one.

The tutor is a rehearsal partner here, not a marking service. It is useful for reading the community kitchen notice aloud at different speeds, for firing nouns at a learner who must answer less or fewer, and for checking whether a phrase kept its small word. Every task in this unit carries its own answer key, so nothing depends on the tutor's opinion.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say less water and fewer bottles, and use both and all.
I can compare how something is done: harder, sooner, the earliest.
I can say by bus, in cash, on foot and at once, and ask about them.
I can turn kind into kindness, and find the two words inside a joined noun.
I can read a notice on my own and find the limits and the times.
I can listen to a short talk and say what its main points were.
I can write a short text by hand, and read every word of it back the next day.

assignment.title: The last three months, in your own words
assignment.instructions:
This is the checkpoint for the stage. Make one recording and write one card by hand. You may invent every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about one and a half minutes.
Talk about the last three months. Use all six of these, at least once each:
for or since, for how long something has been true,
an -ing or -ed describing word, for a thing or for you,
I think or I am sure, with a reason after because,
if plus something that is always true,
was or were plus -ing, cut across by a second action,
and one comparison with harder, sooner, earlier or better.
Add two sentences with less or fewer.
Play it back and count the six. If one is missing, record it again.
Part 2. The card, written by hand.
Write eight lines about how your week works now.
Use three fixed phrases from by bus, on foot, in cash, in person, at once, for free.
Use two nouns for things you cannot touch, and one joined noun.
Use fewer once and less once.
Under the card, write one line that starts: This stage taught me …
Check the card against the four criteria for Writing 3 before you finish.
Put it away and read it again a day later. Every word should still be readable.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and a handwritten card
